# Summary
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) utilize permutation equivariant message passing and pooling to effectively model graph-structured data. Key architectures—including MPNNs, GCNs, GATs, and GGS-NN—address oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophily, and non-isomorphism, enabling applications in computer vision, NLP, protein folding, optimization, and cybersecurity.
Autoencoders, such as vanilla, VAE, sparse, denoising, contractive, β-VAE, CVAE, multi-latent, and adversarial types, provide compact representations that support anomaly detection, semantic hashing, drug discovery, and communications; transformer-based encoding further enhances their capabilities.
Class activation mapping (e.g., Grad-CAM) increases CNN interpretability by visualizing feature saliency, while Radial Basis Function (RBF) networks efficiently approximate functions using clustering and gradient descent, supporting high-dimensional time-series tasks.
Transformers have revolutionized sequence modeling by using attention and feed-forward layers for faster, more scalable training compared to RNNs. Core features include self-attention, feed-forward blocks, residual connections, normalization (LayerNorm, RMSNorm, CapsuleNorm, ScaleNorm, FixNorm), varied positional encodings, and efficient optimization techniques (GELU/SwiGLU activations, learning rate warmup, weight tying, KV caching, FlashAttention, and GPU optimizations). Advanced architectures and efficiency improvements—such as Multi-Query, Grouped-Query, Latent, and speculative attention—enable long-context handling and faster inference. Training paradigms span masked language modeling (BERT), autoregressive modeling (GPT), prefix training, and vision/multimodal extensions supported by TensorFlow, PyTorch, and Hugging Face. Transformers excel at NLP tasks (translation, summarization, code generation, speech-to-text) and have been widely adapted for multimodal workflows, where inputs such as vision and audio are tokenized for transfer learning and state-of-the-art performance. Multimodal architectures like LLaVA, Vision Transformers, Conformer, Whisper, Perceivers, and generative models (DALL-E, Parti, Muse, Phenaki) drive advances in image, video, and speech understanding, as well as biological sequence analysis and chess evaluation.
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)—including LSTM, GRU, IndRNN, and hierarchical forms—encode temporal and spatial patterns for tasks like translation, time-series, speech, and protein prediction. Hopfield Networks, rooted in energy minimization, inform modern attention mechanisms.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), with variants like InfoGAN, CycleGAN, StyleGAN, DCGAN, VAEGAN, TransGAN, and Flow-GAN, facilitate style transfer, multi-scale learning, and invertible augmentation with broad scientific and creative applications, leveraging transfer learning and game-theoretic training with Jensen–Shannon losses.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) employ convolution, pooling, activations, and dense layers, with regularization (dropout, stochastic pooling, augmentation, early stopping, weight constraints) to combat overfitting. Key hyperparameters—padding, stride, filters, pooling, dilation—enable translation equivariance and geometric modeling for vision, recognition, anomaly detection, molecular prediction, strategic games, and 3D archaeology. CNNs benefit from interpretability methods, transfer learning, attention modules, and are supported by frameworks such as Caffe, Deeplearning4j, Dlib, Microsoft Cognitive Toolkit, TensorFlow, Theano, and Torch. Related architectures include DQN, CDBN, and Neural Abstraction Pyramids.
